Mandates can be cancelled, but cancelling a purchase intent is an adjacent control, not versioning or rollback, and does not make the axis applicable.

Visa Intelligent Commerce documents first-party rails for agent-initiated purchases. These include agent-specific network tokens, passkey-authenticated purchase-intent mandates, and credential retrieval scoped to a named merchant and amount. Its Trusted Agent Protocol lets merchants verify agents and receive checkout data, and an MCP server/agent toolkit can create payment links. So an assistant can complete a purchase at a Visa-accepting merchant. However, the evidence never documents a merchant-facing way to list or sell products directly inside named chat surfaces. ChatGPT appears only in a community comment reacting to news, and the product is flagged as still 'in the process of development and deployment.' Missing for 10: documented integrations with ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini/Copilot checkout surfaces, merchant catalog/product exposure to assistants, production availability, and independent hands-on corroboration.

Visa publishes the Trusted Agent Protocol spec openly. It defines required RFC 9421 signature fields, tags, timestamp and nonce rules, and a public JWKS. It ships an open-licensed reference implementation (tap-agent, cdn-proxy verifier, merchant-backend, agent-registry) plus signature-base verification snippets. The Intelligent Commerce REST API is path-versioned (/acp/v1) with documented required fields. However, there is no evidence of a formal machine-readable schema, a protocol versioning or compatibility policy, or a dedicated conformance or validation test suite beyond sample code. The product is also flagged as still 'in the process of development and deployment.' Missing for 10: published machine-readable schema (OpenAPI/JSON Schema), explicit protocol version/compatibility policy, dedicated conformance or validation tooling, independent hands-on corroboration.

Dispute handling is a fair question for an agentic payments platform, so the axis applies. However, the evidence shows no dispute or chargeback API covering evidence submission, status, or outcomes. The docs only describe collecting commerce signals that "can be used to resolve any disputes", and an optional disputePolicy field on credential requests; both are adjacent features, not a dispute-management API.

The FEES & TERMS section says "Free to use in Sandbox. Contact Visa for fees in Production." Production pricing for agent-originated transactions is therefore not published, and merchants must contact Visa to price agentic channels. That is the opposite of what the story asks for.

The Trusted Agent Protocol spec says that when a merchant answers with an HTTP 402 response code, the agent's signed Agentic Payment Container carries a "payment IOU". After verifying it, the merchant can grant access with funds expected at settlement, which is a first-party, UI-less machine-payment path. Its RFC 9421 signed-request rail and open reference implementation support agent-to-server interactions. However, the 402 flow is a single paragraph in the spec, and nothing shows per-call API metering, pricing, or a developer workflow for monetizing a service this way. Missing for 10: documented per-call pricing/metering for APIs, 402 IOU settlement and failure-handling details, a reference implementation or SDK for 402 payment acceptance, and independent or hands-on corroboration of the 402 flow.

Visa's docs describe a documented human approval step before money moves. The user authenticates each Payment Instruction with their Passkey, and purchase-intent mandates carry a consumerPrompt (e.g. 'Authorize payment to Best Buy'), a decline threshold and an expiry. Credential requests and authorizations are then validated against that authenticated instruction, and merchants can verify the user's permission via TAP signatures. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration that the passkey approval flow works in practice, and production maturity (the docs say 'This product is in the process of development and deployment').

However, production use requires contacting Visa, and there is no simple enable-a-setting path. missing for 10: self-serve production onboarding (fees and terms are 'Contact Visa'), a one-click merchant setting or toggle for agent acceptance, independent or hands-on corroboration of merchant onboarding.

The evidence shows Visa publishing the Trusted Agent Protocol as an open spec, aligned with web-bot-auth, with its own reference implementation (agent-registry, cdn-proxy, merchant-backend, tap-agent). It does not document any independent third party implementing the protocol or platform. The only hint of an outside party is a community comment about a ChatGPT integration, which is a single vendor partnership rather than two independent implementations. Openness and a sample ecosystem are building blocks, not proof of an ecosystem.

The Trusted Agent Protocol is the agent-to-merchant protocol Visa Intelligent Commerce uses. Its spec is publicly readable on developer.visa.com and GitHub without credentials, builds on RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures, and ships an open-licensed reference implementation that merchants can implement against Visa's public JWKS. The core Intelligent Commerce payment APIs (/acp/v1 tokens, instructions, credentials) are different: they are credential-gated and require a sandbox sign-up with terms acceptance, and production requires contacting Visa. That means only part of the commerce protocol surface is open to implement without signing anything. Missing for 10: evidence of a formally versioned protocol specification, an openly implementable (non-gated) spec for the payment/credential layer, independent corroboration.

Visa Intelligent Commerce is essentially API-first. Its core lifecycle is documented as REST endpoints: card enrollment via POST /acp/v1/tokens, purchase-intent mandates and cancellation via /acp/v1/instructions, and credential retrieval via /instructions/{id}/credentials. An official MCP server also exposes the APIs to agents. However, there is no explicit UI/API parity claim, sandbox onboarding runs through a self-serve web form with Business Center account instructions sent by email, and dispute handling stops at signal capture rather than an API. Missing for 10: a documented parity statement, API-based onboarding/account provisioning, a dispute/refund API, and independent hands-on confirmation that no action is UI-only.

Data portability is a fair question for a payments platform that stores enrolled cards, tokens, mandates and purchase instructions. However, the evidence documents no bulk export, open-format download, or offboarding path for that data. The openly licensed Trusted Agent Protocol spec and reference implementation show protocol openness, an adjacent feature that is not data export, so it earns no credit.

The open-source Trusted Agent Protocol reference implementation and the locally runnable MCP/agent toolkit are adjacent pieces or clients of the hosted APIs, not a self-hostable deployment of the core product, so they earn no credit.

Visa documents agent-specific network tokens, not raw card numbers, provisioned per user (visa-ic-supp-1). They are bound to a passkey-authenticated purchase-intent mandate with a declineThreshold amount cap and an effectiveUntilTime expiry (visa-ic-supp-3). Credential retrieval must declare the merchant and amount, and VisaNet enforces at authorization that the request comes from the intended merchant for the correct amount; intents can be cancelled (visa-ic-supp-2, visa-ic-supp-5). Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration that these controls are enforced in production, and general availability rather than the documented 'in the process of development and deployment' status.

Missing for 10: documented settlement/payout flows for agent transactions, merchant reporting or reconciliation exports identifying agent-originated payments, evidence of parity with other channels in reconciliation, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

However, caps are scoped per instruction/mandate rather than as standing per-agent budgets, revocation is only shown as cancelling a single intent, and the product is flagged as still in development. Missing for 10: standing per-agent spend caps and frequency/usage limits, an explicit instant revocation of an agent's token or payment authority, independent or hands-on corroboration.
